title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Rail
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: FBI seizes the Chinese state-sponsored platforms that scanned US critical infrastructure and relayed the attacks through hijacked devices
items.content_text: The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures on 26 August of QScan and QTRouter, two linked platforms run by a PRC state-sponsored group the government calls QTFY and ties to a Nanjing contractor. QScan performed reconnaissance against US critical infrastructure; QTRouter relayed the resulting intrusions through compromised routers and IoT devices so traffic arrived from ordinary domestic addresses. Both are now inoperable because the seized domains were hard-coded into the malware for command and authentication. Named victims are federal, and the described activity runs back to at least 2018. For railroads and transit agencies the relay layer is the transferable point: a rail estate is full of small, internet-connected, unpatched devices — and the source address in your logs never proved anything.

_otthreatfeed.category: Top Story
_otthreatfeed.source_name: US Department of Justice press release and unsealed court documents — corroborated by TechCrunch and UPI
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Seizures announced and confirmed 26 Aug 2026; described activity dates from at least 2018 to 2026

items.title: A cyberattack put a rail-served inland port onto manual gate processing
items.content_text: North Carolina Ports confirmed a cyberattack that disrupted IT systems across the Port of Wilmington, the Port of Morehead City and the Charlotte Inland Port, the last of which is a rail-served intermodal facility. The incident was detected on 4 August, the authority activated its cybersecurity contingency plan, and recovery began the next morning with operations moved to manual gate processing. The Coast Guard and state officials monitored the response. For railroads the relevance is the interchange: intermodal volumes depend on a terminal operating system that is not yours, and when it goes down your equipment sits while someone else recovers. No attribution or technical detail has been published.

_otthreatfeed.category: Incident — Intermodal facility disruption
_otthreatfeed.source_name: North Carolina Ports statements — reported by BleepingComputer, The Record, CyberScoop and Maritime Executive
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Attack detected 4 Aug 2026; recovery began 5 Aug 2026; operations largely restored by 7 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

items.title: Treasury sanctions an Iranian intelligence-directed hacking network operating inside US critical infrastructure
items.content_text: The US Treasury designated an Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security-directed hacking network on 24 August as part of a wider action covering nearly 60 Iran-linked people, entities and vessels, with a related State Department reward notice. Treasury states the network has breached and exfiltrated data from US energy companies, defence contractors, healthcare providers, IT firms and banks since at least late 2023. Rail is not named, but the tradecraft described — harvesting credentials, vendor footholds and network documentation — is sector-agnostic, and earlier federal reporting has flagged Iranian-affiliated interest in internet-connected control devices used across transportation. Treat this as a targeting signal rather than an incident notification.
tags: Incident — Nation-state targeting of US critical infrastructure

items.title: An attacker crossed a shared private cellular network from one operator’s site into another’s plant
items.content_text: CERT Polska’s follow-up report describes an intrusion that began at a wind farm and ended at an unrelated combined heat and power plant, where a turbine was taken out of service. The bridge was a private APN both organisations bought from the same carrier. A private APN is an addressing and billing construct, not a security boundary. Railroads and transit agencies should read this closely because cellular is the default connectivity for anything trackside: crossing monitors, signal-house telemetry, defect detectors, remote switch heaters, station equipment and positive train control backhaul. If those devices sit on a shared APN and can address one another, the isolation you assumed may not exist.
tags: Incident — Lateral movement across a shared carrier network

items.title: Researchers used an AI model to port a working PLC exploit to a sibling controller — then bricked one
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs set a large language model the task of taking a working remote-code-execution exploit for one WAGO controller — the 750-852, via CVE-2021-31886, a pre-authentication buffer overflow in its Nucleus FTP server — and re-targeting it at a related model, the 750-831. It worked, but not cheaply or unattended: the final stage alone ran more than eight hours and over $500 in API costs, with a researcher steering throughout. A later session aimed at building a command-and-control implant wrote a payload into flash-mapped memory and permanently bricked the test controller. For rail and transit the relevant detail is fleet uniformity in reverse: wayside, station and depot control estates are assembled from close variants of the same controller families, and an exploit proven on one variant is now materially cheaper to move onto its siblings.
tags: Research — AI-assisted exploit porting against PLCs

_otthreatfeed.category: Research — AI-assisted exploit porting against PLCs
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Forescout Vedere Labs research reported by SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Reported 1 Sep 2026; underlying flaw CVE-2021-31886 disclosed 2021

items.title: NCSC issues an alert: increased targeting of OT across multiple sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
items.content_text: The NCSC published a formal alert on 27 August stating it has seen increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, by a range of threat actors, with some limited real-world disruption already resulting. It names no victims, actors or techniques. Rail is not called out, but the exposure pattern the NCSC describes is the one railways carry structurally: assets spread across hundreds of miles, reached over carrier links, commissioned by integrators, and running long-lived equipment nobody replaces on an IT cycle. The alert’s core instruction — do not assume your OT is unreachable from the internet without verifying it, because exposure comes from misconfiguration, legacy connections and unmanaged assets — applies directly to level-crossing controllers, wayside cabinets, SCADA for traction power and tunnel ventilation, depot and yard systems, and station building management. It also aligns closely with what TSA security directives already require of US passenger and freight carriers.
tags: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting

_otthreatfeed.category: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting
_otthreatfeed.source_name: UK National Cyber Security Centre alert, “Disruptive cyber activity highlights risk from internet-exposed systems and edge devices”

items.title: CISA’s red team took a domain undetected — the tooling was fine, the monitoring was not
items.content_text: CISA advisory AA26-237A publishes paired red-team results from two critical-infrastructure organisations assessed with comparable tradecraft. One detected and responded; the other never noticed a domain compromise. The advisory is direct that the difference was not product spend — both had capable tooling, but only one reviewed the output, correlated identity events and had practised the response. Transit agencies and railroads recognise the pattern because dispatch, maintenance, fare collection and corporate systems so often share one Active Directory, and because operational networks are frequently left outside monitoring on the grounds that the alerts would be too noisy to action.
tags: Threat intel — Federal red-team assessment findings

_otthreatfeed.category: Threat intel — Federal red-team assessment findings

items.title: Five agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers on exposed networks
items.content_text: Joint advisory AA26-231A from NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA describes actors using AI assistance to build custom tooling from a well-documented open-source S7 library, querying internet-exposed Siemens S7 controllers in traffic that resembles legitimate monitoring. The agencies assess the activity as reconnaissance and pre-positioning. Rail is not a named sector, but SIMATIC controllers are widespread in station and depot systems, platform screen doors, traction power auxiliaries, washplants and maintenance facilities. The change that matters is that protocol expertise no longer gates who can interrogate a controller — so an exposed S7 in a depot is being read by a larger population than it was a year ago.
tags: Threat intel — Joint federal advisory on ICS protocol tooling

items.title: 1,140 industrial ransomware victims in a quarter, and none of them needed the control system touched
items.content_text: Dragos counted 1,140 ransomware incidents at industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up around 12 percent on the first, and drew out the point that attackers do not need control-system access to disrupt operations. The rail translation is straightforward: nobody needs to reach a signalling system to degrade a railroad. Encrypting crew calling, work order and maintenance management, car and consist tracking, fare collection or customer information produces delays, cancellations and manual working on its own. Those systems rarely receive the segmentation, backup validation or restoration testing applied to safety-critical signalling.
tags: Threat intel — Quarterly industrial ransomware analysis

items.title: A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in SonicWall’s SMA1000 remote-access gateway is being exploited, and CISA gave agencies three days
items.content_text: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance are being exploited in the wild; the company says it found both the flaws and the exploitation internally. CVE-2026-83548, scored CVSS 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface. CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an operating-system command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console. Chained, the pair gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on the appliance itself. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2 September with a 5 September deadline for federal civilian agencies, and marked both entries as requiring forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 — a signal that patching alone does not close the incident. Affected models are the SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v; SSL-VPN running on SonicWall firewalls and the SMA 100 series are not affected.

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
_otthreatfeed.source_name: SonicWall PSIRT advisory and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 2 Sep 2026 — corroborated by SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security and Sophos
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Vendor advisory published 1 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 2 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA’s 1 September ICS batch is mostly Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
items.content_text: CISA published eight industrial control system advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The one most sites will notice first is ICSA-26-244-01, covering four denial-of-service flaws in RSLinx Classic 4.50 and earlier — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625. All four are remotely triggerable with no authentication and no user interaction: a single crafted Common Industrial Protocol packet crashes the RSLinx Classic service. Rockwell has fixed all four in version 4.60. The rest of the batch covers the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (ICSA-26-244-02), the Logix platform (-03, reaching ControlLogix 5580, CompactLogix 5380, GuardLogix 5580 and Compact GuardLogix 5380), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). No exploitation has been reported for any of them.

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Vendor patch available
_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-244-01 through ICSA-26-244-05, published 1 Sep 2026, cross-checked against the Rockwell Automation security advisory index
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Advisories published 1 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

items.title: Rockwell fixes a weak password-hashing work factor in OTTO Fleet Manager — low drama, but it sits on the AMR control path
items.content_text: Rockwell has patched CVE-2026-75112 in OTTO Fleet Manager, the console that dispatches autonomous mobile robots. CISA lists the product in both the critical manufacturing and transportation systems sectors, which is why it is worth a rail and transit reader’s attention: these fleets increasingly move parts and materials around maintenance-of-way depots, rolling-stock overhaul shops and logistics facilities. The flaw itself is modest — an insufficient bcrypt work factor that lowers the cost of brute-forcing stolen password hashes, scored 6.8 (CVSSv3) / 6.9 (CVSSv4) and not remotely exploitable. The point is inventory rather than urgency: depot automation tends to be procured by facilities or engineering and does not always reach the OT asset register that TSA-directed programmes are built around.
tags: Advisory — Autonomous mobile robot fleet management

_otthreatfeed.category: Advisory — Autonomous mobile robot fleet management
_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-239-03 and the Rockwell Automation security advisory — corroborated by the WaterISAC weekly roundup

items.title: Three more exploited flaws land in KEV — a Linux kernel bug, a JFrog Artifactory path traversal and a two-year-old ownCloud authentication bypass
items.content_text: CISA added three more actively exploited flaws to the KEV catalogue on 27 August, a day after the six-flaw batch that included NetScaler. None is a rail product, and that is the relevant point for a sector whose safety systems are usually well separated but whose operations are not. CVE-2026-53362 is a Linux kernel flaw, and the traffic management server, passenger information system, CCTV recorder, network sensor and many wayside gateways are Linux underneath — often vendor appliances patched on the supplier’s schedule rather than the operator’s. CVE-2026-66384 is a path traversal in JFrog Artifactory, relevant wherever firmware and software builds bound for onboard or wayside equipment are staged. CVE-2023-49105 is an ownCloud authentication bypass patched since late 2023; the instances still exposed tend to be ones no team owns. Wabtec’s data leak this month is a reminder that rail’s IT layer is already being worked.
tags: Advisory — Three additions to the CISA KEV catalogue

_otthreatfeed.category: Advisory — Three additions to the CISA KEV catalogue
_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition, corroborated by Security Affairs and SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Added to KEV 27 Aug 2026; ownCloud flaw originally disclosed Nov 2023

items.title: A seven-year-old SQL Server flaw is now confirmed exploited — and it is the database under your historian
items.content_text: CISA added six vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, and the one that matters most on the plant floor is CVE-2019-1068, a remote code execution flaw in Microsoft SQL Server patched in July 2019 and only now confirmed as exploited in the wild. Successful exploitation runs code under the SQL Server Database Engine service account; where that account is over-privileged — which is common on systems installed by an integrator years ago — the attacker moves off the database and onto the Windows host. For a railroad or transit agency this is the database tier under asset management, the SCADA and signalling historian, the fare-collection back office and the maintenance records — commonly SQL Server instances that a systems integrator stood up during a capital project and that nobody has patched since the project closed out. No public write-up of the in-the-wild technique has appeared, so detection guidance is thin; the federal remediation deadline is 29 August. Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-8452 was added in the same batch.
tags: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, historian and MES databases

items.title: The NetScaler flaw is now confirmed exploited and in KEV — federal deadline 29 August
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-8452 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, moving the Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway issue from a patching recommendation to confirmed exploitation in the wild. It is a heap overflow in SAML single sign-on parsing, rated CVSS 8.8, needing no authentication, and reachable when the appliance is configured as a Gateway or AAA virtual server. Canada’s Cyber Centre reported indications of exploitation from around 17 August after a public proof of concept. In rail and transit organisations NetScaler frequently fronts the remote access used by dispatch support staff, maintenance contractors and signalling suppliers.
tags: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, remote access

_otthreatfeed.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, remote access
_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition of 26 Aug 2026 and Citrix security bulletin — corroborated by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and watchTowr Labs analysis
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Vendor patches released August 2026; exploitation indications from 17 Aug; added to KEV 26 Aug 2026; federal deadline 29 Aug 2026

items.title: Two unauthenticated flaws in Veeam ONE 13 — the monitoring layer that watches the backups you would restore from
items.content_text: Veeam disclosed vulnerabilities in Veeam ONE 13 in knowledge-base articles published on 25 August. CVE-2026-64633 is rated CVSS v4.0 10.0 and allows remote, unauthenticated code execution on the Veeam ONE agent host; CVE-2026-65641 is rated 9.3 and lets a remote unauthenticated attacker coerce SMB authentication out of the Veeam ONE service account, which is the first step in relaying that account somewhere more useful. Veeam ONE 13.x is affected and the 12.x line is not. For rail and transit, Veeam ONE is often the console watching backups of the SCADA, signalling-adjacent and asset-management servers — the recovery capability behind any incident that would otherwise mean running on manual authorities and paper procedures. There is no report of exploitation yet, but backup and monitoring servers are a standing target precisely because compromising them removes the recovery option before the ransomware runs.
tags: Advisory — Backup and monitoring infrastructure, unauthenticated

items.title: A Git server exploit in KEV — and it is where signalling and station configuration often lives
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-60004 to the KEV catalogue on 25 August after reports of active exploitation. Rated CVSS 9.8, the flaw lets anyone with ordinary repository write access plant an executable Git hook and run shell commands as the Gitea service account. Gitea 1.27.1 fixed it on 27 July, so exploitation followed within a month. Self-hosted Gitea turns up in rail engineering groups because it is easy to stand up for station and depot PLC projects, SCADA screens, passenger information configuration and integration scripts. A modest contractor account then becomes code execution on the machine holding operational configuration. Federal remediation was due 28 August.
tags: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, engineering toolchain

items.title: August ICS Patch Tuesday: Ruggedcom and Desigo alongside a maximum-severity IoT2050 flaw
items.content_text: Siemens published ten advisories in its August set, alongside Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact, with CISA issuing companion ICS advisories the same week. The headline item is a maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices allowing unauthenticated remote code execution with elevated privileges. Rail estates are exposed to more of this batch than most sectors, because Siemens equipment spans the environment: Ruggedcom networking in signal houses and substations, Desigo building automation at stations and depots, Siveillance video management, and SIMATIC controllers in auxiliary and depot systems. Review the whole set rather than only the maximum-severity entry.
tags: Advisory — August ICS Patch Tuesday, Siemens estate

items.title: CISA advisory on a heavy-vehicle brake controller — exploitation costs ABS, traction control and the speedometer
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-237-05 on 25 August covering the Bendix EC80 brake electronic control unit, used in heavy commercial vehicles. According to the advisory, successful exploitation could cause loss of anti-lock braking functions, steering assist, the speedometer and shifting capability, or disable automatic traction control. This lands on the rail and transit page because most transit agencies are also bus operators, and the same vehicle-network exposure applies to the non-revenue and maintenance fleet that supports rail operations. Foundation braking is unaffected — the failure modes described are the electronic assistance layered on top of it — but a bus losing ABS and traction control in service is a safety event, not a maintenance one. Mitigation is a vehicle-network access and firmware question rather than a patch you apply centrally.
tags: Advisory — Commercial vehicle braking ECU, safety functions

items.title: No login required and no patch coming — the Ebyte gateway advisory is a replacement decision
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-237-06 covers the Ebyte NE2-D11 serial-to-Ethernet gateway, whose web management interface does not consistently enforce authentication before granting administrative functionality. An unauthenticated remote attacker can read configuration, change settings, hijack sessions or disrupt operation. CISA notes the vendor acknowledged the reports, said a patch was in development, then stopped responding. Low-cost serial converters of this class are common across rail estates, sitting behind older equipment at crossings, in signal houses, at fuelling points and in depot test rigs — installed because something legacy needed a network connection, and rarely recorded anywhere afterwards.
tags: Advisory — Serial-to-Ethernet gateway, no vendor patch

items.title: Britain moves to bar designated high-risk suppliers from critical infrastructure — without naming them publicly
items.content_text: The UK government has tabled late amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill that would let ministers stop critical-sector organisations from using technology suppliers designated as high risk. The Bill, introduced in November 2025 and now near the end of its passage through the Lords, already extends duties to energy, water, transport and health operators and pulls managed service providers, data centres and digital infrastructure into scope. The amendments were tabled on 24 August and reported on 2 September; they follow reporting that a small UK generating station ran manually for four days after a cyberattack. Designations would not necessarily be made public, which is the detail operators should notice: a supplier could be designated without a public list to check against, so the obligation to know your own supply chain moves from good practice to compliance exposure. None of this is in force yet, and the Bill has not completed its passage.
tags: Regulation & Policy — Proposed, not yet in force

_otthreatfeed.category: Regulation & Policy — Proposed, not yet in force
_otthreatfeed.source_name: SecurityWeek reporting on the amendments tabled to the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Amendments tabled 24 Aug 2026; reported 2 Sep 2026; not yet in force — verified 3 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA publishes internet exposure reduction guidance — and the target list for this sector is wayside cabinets on cellular backhaul, station building-management and CCTV networks, depot engineering access and yard-automation systems
items.content_text: CISA released guidance on 26 August directing organisations to identify which of their systems are reachable from the internet, remove remote access that is not required, and harden whatever must stay externally accessible. It is deliberately unglamorous: an inventory step, a removal step and a hardening step, published in the same week the UK NCSC warned that internet-exposed OT and edge devices are being targeted with real-world disruption already caused. Rail and transit estates are geographically strung out and frequently connected by third-party carrier links, which is exactly the exposure class the guidance describes. Wayside and station equipment is often commissioned by an integrator and inherited by an operator who never received the connectivity diagram. The guidance carries no deadline and applies to no one by force, which is precisely why it tends to be filed rather than executed.
tags: Guidance — Internet exposure reduction for IT, OT and ICS

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Guidance published 26 Aug 2026; reported 27 Aug 2026

items.title: The TSA rail directive runs to 15 January 2027 while the surface cyber rule remains proposed
items.content_text: Security Directive 1580-21-01E, the current TSA cybersecurity directive for designated freight and passenger railroads, is effective from 16 January 2026 through 15 January 2027. Its performance-based requirements — network segmentation between IT and OT, access control, continuous monitoring and timely patching, together with a cybersecurity implementation plan and assessment programme — remain the operative obligation. The broader “Enhancing Surface Cyber Risk Management” rulemaking, published for comment in November 2024 and closed to comment in February 2025, would convert the directives into permanent regulation including 24-hour incident reporting to CISA, but no final rule has been issued.
tags: Policy — TSA rail security directive and pending rulemaking

items.title: From 11 September 2026 exploited vulnerabilities in digital products must be reported within 24 hours
items.content_text: The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations begin on 11 September 2026. Manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must notify an actively exploited vulnerability in their product, or a severe incident affecting its security, within 24 hours of becoming aware, with fuller reporting to follow. Railways sit on both sides of this. Operators buying rolling stock, signalling and station systems from European suppliers gain a defined notification obligation to write into contracts; operators or subsidiaries that themselves place connected products on the EU market acquire the obligation directly.
tags: Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligation

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Regulation entered into force 10 Dec 2024; reporting obligations apply from 11 Sep 2026; full application 11 Dec 2027; status verified 27 Aug 2026

items.title: The NSA is putting an ISA/IEC 62443 certificate in front of the controllers it buys
items.content_text: ISASecure announced a partnership with the National Security Agency to develop a High Criticality Component Security Assurance certification scheme, derived from its Component Security Assurance programme and grounded in ISA/IEC 62443-4-2. Once accepted, the NSA intends to use it when adding OT components to the National Security Systems product compliant list. Rail is not the target market, but the mechanism is what matters: a large buyer making certification a purchase condition changes what vendors build, and the language migrates into other specifications. For an agency writing a station systems or depot automation tender, that is a citable standard rather than an invented requirement.

_otthreatfeed.category: Policy — Procurement-driven security certification
_otthreatfeed.source_name: ISA / ISASecure press release — corroborated by Automation World and ISSSource
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Announced 20 Aug 2026; verified 27 Aug 2026
